title_en: Silver Surfers Club Teaches Older Residents to Go Online
title_ru: Клуб «Серебряные сёрферы» учит пожилых жителей пользоваться интернетом
description_ru: Вымышленная новость: в городке Хартсворт бывший учитель создала бесплатный компьютерный клуб для пожилых, и он изменил их жизнь.
text:
For most of his life, seventy-eight-year-old Bernard Pike never touched a computer. He spent forty years as a bus driver in the town of Hartsworth, and when he retired he said that he would never need one. Today, however, he is the star of a free computer club that has taught more than four hundred older people to use the internet, and he has written his own small program that lets his grandchildren draw pictures on his screen. "I thought that I was too old," he said. "I was wrong."

The Silver Surfers club began two years ago in a cold church hall. Its founder, a former primary school teacher called Margaret Oyelaran, noticed that many of her neighbours were feeling left behind. Banks were closing their branches, bus timetables had moved onto websites, and relatives were sending photographs that the neighbours could not open. "A lot of older people were embarrassed," she said. "They did not want to ask for help, and so they stayed at home." She asked the local library to lend her six old laptops, and she placed a notice in a shop window. Eleven people came to the first lesson.

Since then the club has grown rapidly. It now meets three times a week in the library, and it has a waiting list of almost sixty people. The volunteers who run the lessons include students, office workers and even a few teenagers who have come after school. Some members have never used a mouse, so the first lesson is usually about clicking and typing. After that, students learn how to send emails, make video calls, shop safely online and avoid the scams that trick so many people. "The first time my daughter appeared on the screen, I cried," said Doris Lindqvist, who is eighty-four. "She lives in another country, and I had not seen her face for two years."

The club has also had an unexpected benefit: friendship. Many of the members live alone, and the lessons, which end with tea and cake, have become the highlight of their week. Researchers at Hartsworth University have studied the group for several months, and they have found that members report feeling less lonely and more confident than before. "Technology can seem cold," said Dr Anita Rowe, who led the study, "but if people learn it together, it can bring them closer."

Learning has not always been easy. The most common problem, say the volunteers, is fear. Some members worry that they will break the computer by pressing the wrong key, while others are afraid of being tricked by criminals. To help them, the club has a famous rule: "If you make a mistake, say sorry to the computer and try again." Bernard Pike, who is now one of the volunteer teachers, says that it works. "I once deleted all my photographs by accident," he said. "I nearly gave up, but the others laughed, helped me find them, and made me a cup of tea."

The council has noticed the club's success. Last month, it offered a grant of five thousand pounds so that the group can buy new laptops and pay for a bigger room. Councillor Dorothy Venn said that the programme saved the town money by helping older people to book appointments and pay bills without travelling. "If every town had a club like this, we would have fewer lonely people and fewer missed doctors' appointments," she said. Other towns have already asked how they can copy it, and Ms Oyelaran has agreed to write a short guide that explains the idea.

The youngest volunteers say that they have learned just as much as the members. Fifteen-year-old Kofi Mensah, who helps on Wednesday afternoons, said that explaining things slowly had improved his own understanding. "Older people ask very good questions," he said. "They always want to know why something works, not only which button to press." Several of the teenagers have already decided that they would like to become teachers.

Not everyone is enthusiastic. A few members believe that older people should not be pushed into using technology, and they argue that banks and public offices should still provide paper forms and face-to-face help. Ms Oyelaran agrees. "Nobody should be forced," she said. "But if somebody wants to learn, it should be easy and free."

Next month, the club will hold its first graduation ceremony. Fourteen students will receive certificates, and Bernard Pike has promised to give a speech. He has already practised it on a video call with his grandchildren. "I will tell them that you are never too old to learn," he said, smiling. "And then I will ask them how to turn the microphone on."
